content: Yes, we will record, and baring any complications will post on the Lean FRO YouTube channel.
2 messages were moved here from #Event announcements > Panel Series: The Proof in the Code by Floris van Doorn.

Let's use this thread as a discussion thread for both the book and the panel discussions.
Panel announcement: #Event announcements > Panel Series: The Proof in the Code
Publisher link for the book: https://www.quantabooks.org/books/the-proof-in-the-code/

Given that the book came out yesterday, I bought the audiobook myself, and I've been enjoying listening to it. It's very nice to relive the story of Lean from multiple perspectives, and I'm enjoying it a lot so far!

Wonderful book! I don't often listen to audiobooks but I had a free credit and now I can't stop listening. I'm looking forward to seeing how it is received, by both the general public and the math community. My only nitpick is that there was a brief discussion of constructivism early on which didn't get things quite right, IMHO.
I was not impressed by some of the framing and editorial choices in the sample posted on Quanta's website
This article says it is adapted from the book: https://www.quantamagazine.org/how-terry-tao-became-an-evangelist-for-ai-in-math-20260608/

Literally nowhere in the article does it start addressing the title: the only relevant mention of the of AI in mathematics was a quote Terry admitting he would use a little AI help in his process of learning Lean.

There are other rhetorical devices used as early as the first paragraph that if I were an editor I would make the author rewrite it.
(I have been a beta reader on a novel, and my feedback in referee reports is always _very_ detailed.)

What I took from the article was that Tao thought that LLMs are unreliable, but that there's a path to using them productively by using formal verification to check their outputs, in the same way that FV can be used to coordinate large scale math projects like equational theories.

I think this is the YouTube video for the panel the article discusses, I was struck that around 28:32 Jacob Lurie talks about what is being referred to nowadays as "digestion" and says it's undervalued.

This seems like important evidence that mathematicians have long seen this component as needful.

David Michael Roberts said:

Literally nowhere in the article does it start addressing the title: the only relevant mention of the of AI in mathematics was a quote Terry admitting he would use a little AI help in his process of learning Lean.

If you change the word "AI" in the title to "Computers" then the title matches the text fairly well. I can imagine (though I'm not claiming this is what really happened) the author using the word "Computers" and then an editor changing "Computers" to "AI" to make it more "catchy," figuring that the two words are semantically interchangeable.

I'm only about halfway through the book so far, but overall I think Hartnett did a great job. Not many writers would bother to mention Llull or even Leibniz, for example, and Hartnett's explanations of technical concepts are generally accurate and clear (a more difficult achievement than most people realize). I did find some of the comments about set theory, shall we say, puzzling; e.g., given the existence of Metamath Zero, I don't see how set theory is inconsistent with a "taste for minimality" (p.49). I also wish there were some mention of the consistency of NF, but one can't have everything...

I finished listening to the audiobook version of the book and like it a lot. I particularly enjoyed the personal and sociological depictions. The Quanta Magazine excerpt that Chris pointed to above is actually rather unrepresentative, because it comes from the 10th chapter of an 11-chapter book and I certainly would not consider Tao to be a major character in the narrative arc of the book.
Is the book available somewhere as an ebook without DRM?

Read it today--overall a very interesting read! I only came to Lean in the Lean 4 era so it was super cool to learn about the history. It steps on a couple of landmines (claims that a constructive proof of the Goldbach conjecture is impossible because it would involve computing infinitely many examples...) but overall I think a few errors are forgivable given the audience. Much better read than the blurb would suggest!
